elements.name: CAS Retry Loop
elements.what: Read a shared word, compute a new value, and attempt to install it with compare-and-swap, looping until the CAS succeeds.
elements.problem: Allows atomic read-modify-write of shared state without locks; contention is absorbed by retrying instead of blocking, giving lock-free progress.
elements.named_in: The Art of Multiprocessor Programming - Herlihy & Shavit (2008)

elements.name: ABA Mitigation via Tagged Pointer
elements.what: Pair the CAS-protected word with a monotonically increasing tag/version so a value that was changed and changed back still fails the CAS.
elements.problem: Plain CAS cannot distinguish 'unchanged' from 'changed A->B->A', which corrupts lock-free structures that recycle nodes; the tag makes every mutation observable.
elements.named_in: The Art of Multiprocessor Programming - Herlihy & Shavit (2008)

elements.name: Hazard Pointers
elements.what: Each thread publishes single-writer pointers naming the nodes it is currently accessing; reclaimers defer freeing any node named in a hazard pointer.
elements.problem: Safe memory reclamation for lock-free data structures: a node removed from the structure may still be dereferenced by a concurrent reader, so freeing must wait until no reader can hold it.
elements.named_in: Hazard Pointers: Safe Memory Reclamation for Lock-Free Objects - Maged M. Michael (2004)

elements.name: Epoch-Based Reclamation
elements.what: Threads announce a global epoch on entering read-side sections; retired nodes are freed only after all threads have advanced past the epoch in which the nodes were retired.
elements.problem: Amortizes the cost of safe memory reclamation for lock-free structures: per-access publication (as in hazard pointers) is replaced by cheap per-critical-section epoch bookkeeping.
elements.named_in: Practical Lock-Freedom (UCAM-CL-TR-579) - Keir Fraser (2004)

elements.name: Read-Copy-Update
elements.what: Readers traverse shared data with no locks or atomics; updaters publish new versions by pointer swap and defer freeing old versions until every reader passes a quiescent state (grace period).
elements.problem: Read-mostly shared data where reader overhead must be near zero; converts the reclamation question into detecting that all pre-existing readers have finished.
elements.named_in: Read-Copy Update: Using Execution History to Solve Concurrency Problems - McKenney & Slingwine (1998)

elements.name: Sequence Lock
elements.what: A writer increments a sequence counter before and after updating; readers retry their lock-free read if the counter was odd or changed across the read.
elements.problem: Lets many readers access small, frequently-read data without locking while guaranteeing they never act on a torn/inconsistent snapshot; writers never wait for readers.
elements.named_in: Sequence counters and sequential locks - Linux kernel documentation (locking/seqlock.rst)

elements.name: Ticket Lock
elements.what: A spinlock built from two counters: acquirers atomically take a ticket and spin until the now-serving counter reaches it.
elements.problem: Test-and-set spinlocks are unfair and cause contention storms; the ticket discipline grants the lock in strict FIFO order with one atomic op per acquisition.
elements.named_in: Algorithms for Scalable Synchronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors - Mellor-Crummey & Scott (1991)

elements.name: MCS Queue Lock
elements.what: Waiters enqueue a per-thread node and spin only on their own node's flag; the releaser hands the lock to its queue successor.
elements.problem: Global-spin locks generate cache-coherence traffic proportional to waiters; local spinning on a private cache line makes acquisition scalable and FIFO-fair on many-core machines.
elements.named_in: Algorithms for Scalable Synchronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors - Mellor-Crummey & Scott (1991)

elements.name: Test-and-Test-and-Set Lock
elements.what: Spin reading the lock word from cache until it appears free, and only then attempt the atomic test-and-set; typically combined with exponential backoff between attempts.
elements.problem: Naive test-and-set spinning hammers the bus with atomic operations; spinning on a cached read plus backoff bounds coherence traffic under contention.
elements.named_in: The Art of Multiprocessor Programming - Herlihy & Shavit (2008)

elements.name: Futex
elements.what: Synchronization objects keep their state in a plain userspace word manipulated with atomics; the kernel is invoked only to sleep on or wake waiters when the fast path fails.
elements.problem: Uncontended lock and unlock should cost one atomic instruction with zero syscalls, while contended waiters still block properly instead of spinning.
elements.named_in: Fuss, Futexes and Furwocks: Fast Userlevel Locking in Linux - Franke, Russell & Kirkwood (2002)
elements.borderline: Kernel-assisted: the mechanism spans a syscall boundary, but the design element (userspace fast path + kernel wait queue keyed by address) is implemented inside one component and recurs across runtimes.

elements.name: Lock-Free FIFO Queue (Michael-Scott)
elements.what: A linked-list MPMC queue where enqueue and dequeue advance head/tail with CAS, and threads help complete a lagging tail swing before proceeding.
elements.problem: A shared FIFO whose operations never block: no lock-holder preemption stalls, safe in mixed-priority and signal contexts, scalable under moderate contention.
elements.named_in: Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms - Michael & Scott (1996)

elements.name: Lock-Free Stack (Treiber)
elements.what: A linked LIFO where push and pop swing the top-of-stack pointer with a CAS retry loop (with an ABA guard when nodes are recycled).
elements.problem: The minimal lock-free container: a shared free list or work stack usable from contexts where locking is forbidden or unscalable.
elements.named_in: Systems Programming: Coping with Parallelism (IBM Research Report RJ 5118) - R. K. Treiber (1986)

elements.name: SPSC Lock-Free Ring Buffer
elements.what: A bounded circular buffer where one producer owns the write index and one consumer owns the read index, so each side progresses wait-free with only acquire/release ordering and no atomic RMW.
elements.problem: Passing data between exactly two threads (or thread and ISR) with minimal, bounded, allocation-free overhead; the ownership split removes the need for locks or CAS entirely.
elements.named_in: Proving the Correctness of Multiprocess Programs - Leslie Lamport (1977)

elements.name: Memory Barrier
elements.what: An explicit instruction or compiler directive that constrains the order in which memory operations before and after it may become visible to other processors.
elements.problem: Compilers and CPUs reorder memory accesses; lockless code communicating through shared memory must pin down ordering at the points where publication and observation happen.
elements.named_in: Linux kernel memory-barriers.txt - McKenney, Howells et al. (Linux kernel documentation)
elements.borderline: Sits at the hardware/language floor of the band, but barrier placement discipline is a named, recurring design activity in every lockless codebase, distinct from the raw instruction.

elements.name: Acquire-Release Ordering
elements.what: Pair a release-ordered store by the producer with an acquire-ordered load by the consumer so everything written before the release is visible after the acquire, without full fences.
elements.problem: Sequentially-consistent atomics are needlessly expensive for the common publish/consume handoff; the acquire-release pair expresses exactly the one-way visibility the handoff needs.
elements.named_in: Acquire and Release Semantics - Jeff Preshing (2012)
elements.borderline: Codified as language memory-model vocabulary (C++11/C11), but used as a portable design discipline for lockless handoff rather than a single-keyword feature.

elements.name: False-Sharing Avoidance via Cache-Line Padding
elements.what: Pad or align independently-written shared variables so no two of them share a cache line.
elements.problem: False sharing: logically independent data co-resident in one cache line causes coherence-protocol ping-pong that silently serializes unrelated threads.
elements.named_in: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory - Ulrich Drepper (2007)

elements.name: Per-CPU Data Sharding
elements.what: Replicate a shared datum (counter, pool, cache) into one instance per CPU or thread so the fast path touches only local, uncontended memory, aggregating across shards only when a global view is needed.
elements.problem: Any centrally-updated shared variable becomes a scalability bottleneck; partitioning by executor eliminates synchronization and coherence traffic on the hot path.
elements.named_in: Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It? - Paul E. McKenney (perfbook)

elements.name: Lock Striping
elements.what: Guard a single logical structure with an array of locks, hashing each element or bucket to one stripe so independent operations proceed in parallel.
elements.problem: One coarse lock over a large structure serializes all access; striping trades a bounded set of locks for near-linear reduction in contention without per-element lock overhead.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz et al. (2006)

elements.name: Software Transactional Memory
elements.what: Shared-memory operations are grouped into transactions that execute speculatively against a log or versioned words and commit atomically, aborting and retrying on conflict.
elements.problem: Composing fine-grained locking is error-prone (deadlock, lock ordering); STM gives composable atomic blocks with optimistic conflict detection instead of programmer-managed locks.
elements.named_in: Software Transactional Memory - Shavit & Touitou (1995)

elements.name: Optimistic Concurrency via Version Validation
elements.what: Proceed without locks, recording versions of the data read; at commit time re-check the versions and retry the whole operation if anything changed.
elements.problem: When conflicts are rare, pessimistic locking pays its cost on every access; optimistic validation moves the cost to the rare conflicting case.
elements.named_in: On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control - Kung & Robinson (1981)

elements.name: Flat Combining
elements.what: Threads publish operation requests to a shared list; one thread acquires a global lock and applies everyone's pending operations in a batch on their behalf.
elements.problem: Under high contention, N threads fighting for a structure cost more than one thread doing N operations; combining turns synchronization overhead into cheap sequential batching.
elements.named_in: Flat Combining and the Synchronization-Parallelism Tradeoff - Hendler, Incze, Shavit & Tzafrir (2010)

elements.name: Restartable Sequences
elements.what: Short userspace critical sections over per-CPU data registered with the kernel, which aborts and restarts the sequence if the thread is preempted or migrated mid-section.
elements.problem: Per-CPU fast paths in userspace cannot otherwise know they stayed on one CPU; rseq gives atomic-free per-CPU updates at the cost of a restartable code discipline.
elements.named_in: Restartable sequences - LWN.net (2015)
elements.borderline: Kernel-assisted like futex: the abort protocol needs kernel cooperation, but the element is a userspace code-structuring mechanism recurring in allocators and libc.

elements.name: Eventcount
elements.what: A monotonically increasing counter that threads can read, advance, and await reaching a value, letting a lock-free fast path add blocking ('sleep until something changed') without locks.
elements.problem: Pure lock-free algorithms busy-wait when empty; an eventcount lets consumers block on a condition over lock-free state without introducing a mutex into the producer path.
elements.named_in: Synchronization with Eventcounts and Sequencers - Reed & Kanodia (1979)

parked_architecture.name: Shared-nothing architecture
parked_architecture.why: Per-CPU/per-thread sharding scaled to whole-system partitioning (Stonebraker's shared-nothing) is a statement of system structure, not an in-component mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Atomic RMW primitives (CAS/LL-SC/fetch-and-add instructions)
excluded_notable.why: Raw hardware/language primitives below the band; the in-scope elements are the idioms built on them (CAS retry loop, tagged pointer).

excluded_notable.name: Progress-guarantee taxonomy (wait-free / lock-free / obstruction-free)
excluded_notable.why: Classification vocabulary (Herlihy), not an implementable mechanism; belongs in prose/notes, not as an element.

excluded_notable.name: Hardware memory-consistency models (TSO, x86-TSO, ARM weak ordering)
excluded_notable.why: Properties of hardware, not designable elements; the designable counterparts (barrier placement, acquire-release) are included.

notes: Coverage decisions: (1) SPSC ring buffer kept SEPARATE from the generic circular buffer (data-flow scout's element) because the mechanism here is the wait-free split-index ownership protocol (Lamport 1977), not the storage layout - merge step should cross-link them. (2) Algorithm variants folded per rules: CLH lock folded into MCS aka; elimination-backoff stack folded into Treiber stack; hazard eras/interval-based reclamation treated as variants of hazard pointers/EBR; DCAS/DWCAS treated as an implementation of the tagged-pointer ABA guard; qspinlock folded into MCS aka. (3) RCU entry carries QSBR as aka with the quiescent-state note in 'what'. (4) Deliberate overlaps flagged for merge: lock-striping and per-CPU sharding may also surface from a general concurrency/JCiP scout; optimistic-concurrency-version-validation overlaps the db scout (charter says include). (5) Left to other scouts: double-checked locking, monitor object, read-write lock and the POSA2 concurrency patterns (posa2 is in corpus); general thread-pool/executor mechanisms. (6) Borderline kernel-assisted items (futex, rseq) and language-memory-model items (memory barrier, acquire-release) included with borderline rationale per over-inclusion rule. Spot-checks this session: Linux kernel seqlock.rst (docs.kernel.org/locking/seqlock.html), Fraser UCAM-CL-TR-579, Reed & Kanodia CACM 1979 (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/359060.359076), LWN Restartable sequences (lwn.net/Articles/650333/).
